messages.author: 333f3e76f253995a
messages.subject: extended.pgls and trajectory.analysis
parts:
Dear geomorph community,

I am working on a phylogenetic control requested by reviewers, and I would like to know whether extended.pgls() can be combined with trajectory.analysis().

My data and design
- Multivariate shape data (48 variables) for 195 individuals of 6 species, with many individuals per species.
- Species = species (factor); Stage = an ordered three-level factor (e.g., low, medium and high wear: S1, S2, S3). The goal is to build one trajectory per species, with the three stages as trajectory points, and to compare trajectories among species (length, direction, shape).
- Phylogeny: a pruned cladogram with branch lengths assigned (Grafen), with tips matching the levels of Species.

What I did

Ordinary model (works as expected):

fit_ordinary <- procD.lm(Y ~ Species * Stage, data = my_data, iter = 999)
TA_ordinary <- trajectory.analysis(fit_ordinary, groups = my_data$Species,
                                   traj.pts = my_data$Stage, pca = TRUE)

Here the trajectory points are exactly equal to the species-by-stage means of the individual scores in the PC space returned by plot(TA_ordinary).

Phylogenetic model:

fit_phylo <- extended.pgls(Y ~ Species * Stage, data = my_data,
                           species = "Species", phy = my_tree, iter = 999)
TA_phylo <- trajectory.analysis(fit_phylo, groups = my_data$Species,
                                traj.pts = my_data$Stage, pca = TRUE)

trajectory.analysis() runs without errors, but the trajectory points do not match the data. For example, for one species (Species_A), comparing the mean of the individual scores in each stage with the trajectory point, both in the PC space of TA_phylo:

          mean of individuals       trajectory point
          PC1       PC2             PC1       PC2
S1       -0.257     0.060          -2.609     0.061
S2       -0.141     0.030          -1.802    -0.431
S3        0.249     0.134           2.423     0.585

My questions
1. Is trajectory.analysis() intended to work with objects of class lm.rrpp.ws returned by extended.pgls()? If not, is there a recommended way to run a trajectory analysis conditioned on the phylogeny when each trajectory corresponds to a different species?
2. Is there any  limitation when the groups used for the trajectories (Species) are also the species used in the phylogenetic covariance structure?

Some cells are small (for example, n = 2 individuals in a few species-by-stage combinations), in case this is relevant.

I can provide a reproducible example or share the data  if that would help.

Thank you very much for your time.

Best regards,
Ale

geomorph_4.1.1
RRPP_2.2.0

parts:
Ale,

Yes, trajectory.analysis can work with extended.pgls/lm.rrpp.ws.  In our 2024 paper where we introduced extended PGLS, we did precisely that in the pupfish example: extended PGLS + TA.

However, I can replicate the shift in group means in the plot that you described, so a bug seems to have been introduced somewhere. 

We will investigate that.

Dean

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] extended.pgls and trajectory.analysis
parts:
Dear Ale, and everyone,

The issue was caused by a missing phylogenetic transformation of the model matrix used to obtain least-squares means in the RRPP::pairwise function, used within trajectory.analysis (not extended.pgls).  I am hopeful this would cause no major issues with the trajectory analysis, itself, but just the resulting graph.  Phylogenetic transformations were used to obtain random pseudo-data via RRPP and the model matrix for LS means was constructed properly, but not having the phylogenetic transformation in the last step meant the LS means were shifted away from the origin in the PC plot.  This would be a consistent (affine) shift in each RRPP permutation.

Please re-install RRPP from my Gtihub (mlcollyer/RRPP) and see if your results make sense.  Let me know if issues persist.  I will soon send an update to CRAN, but wish to test the function more first.

Sorry for the bug!

Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] extended.pgls and trajectory.analysis
parts:
Dear Dean and Mike,
First of all, thank you very much for your previous feedback and assistance. While the RRPP update resolved the previous issue, I have now encountered another query regarding the Species main effect in E-PGLS.
While analyzing my data, I noticed that the main effect for Species returns a p-value of 1, a very low Z-score (strongly negative), and an R2 approx 0.
To verify whether this was related to my dataset, I ran the PupFishExample-DRYAD.R script provided in the Dryad repository using the current version of RRPP/geomorph. Interestingly, running manova.update(fit) on the pupfish dataset also yields a p-value of 1.000 and Z = -31.60 for Species, whereas Table 1 in the paper reports p = 0.020 and Z = 2.221 (while the remaining terms like Sex, Population, and Species:Sex are very similar to the published table).
Could you provide some guidance on:
    1. Whether this p = 1 result for Species in the latest package version is the expected mathematical outcome?
    2. How we should properly interpret and report a p = 1 for the Species main effect in E-PGLS comparative studies when cross-species interaction terms (Species:Factor) are the main focus of interest?
Thank you again for your time, support
Best regards,
Ale

Dear Ale,

Gah!  This issue popped up recently, I fixed it, and now it seems it has reverted to the errored code.  I will update this again.  For reasons I cannot explain, it seems Github ignores some updates I know I made.  The problem for this is that due to a coding error (literally a mistake to use the number 3 instead of 2), the permutation schedule for the species effect does not get changed from type II - within species blocks.  Therefore, every permutation, the species means are exactly the same.  We want this for other effects but not species effects.  The P-value of 1 is because of invariance in F-stats produced.

I'll update this probably within 15 profanity-laden minutes.

Mike

On Nov 5, 2026, at 2:00 PM, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:

Dear Ale,

Gah!  This issue popped up recently, I fixed it, and now it seems it has reverted to the errored code.  I will update this again.  For reasons I cannot explain, it seems Github ignores some updates I know I made.  The problem for this is that due to a coding error (literally a mistake to use the number 3 instead of 2), the permutation schedule for the species effect does not get changed from type II - within species blocks.  Therefore, every permutation, the species means are exactly the same.  We want this for other effects but not species effects.  The P-value of 1 is because of invariance in F-stats produced.

I'll update this probably within 15 profanity-laden minutes.

Mike

On Nov 5, 2026, at 1:43 PM, alej...@gmail.com <alej...@gmail.com> wrote:

Dear Dean and Mike,
First of all, thank you very much for your previous feedback and assistance. While the RRPP update resolved the previous issue, I have now encountered another query regarding the Species main effect in E-PGLS.
While analyzing my data, I noticed that the main effect for Species returns a p-value of 1, a very low Z-score (strongly negative), and an R2 approx 0.
To verify whether this was related to my dataset, I ran the PupFishExample-DRYAD.R script provided in the Dryad repository using the current version of RRPP/geomorph. Interestingly, running manova.update(fit) on the pupfish dataset also yields a p-value of 1.000 and Z = -31.60 for Species, whereas Table 1 in the paper reports p = 0.020 and Z = 2.221 (while the remaining terms like Sex, Population, and Species:Sex are very similar to the published table).
Could you provide some guidance on:
    1. Whether this p = 1 result for Species in the latest package version is the expected mathematical outcome?
    2. How we should properly interpret and report a p = 1 for the Species main effect in E-PGLS comparative studies when cross-species interaction terms (Species:Factor) are the main focus of interest?
Thank you again for your time, support
Best regards,
Ale


El miércoles, 4 de noviembre de 2026 a las 20:06:18 UTC-3, mlco...@gmail.com escribió:
Dear Ale, and everyone,

The issue was caused by a missing phylogenetic transformation of the model matrix used to obtain least-squares means in the RRPP::pairwise function, used within trajectory.analysis (not extended.pgls).  I am hopeful this would cause no major issues with the trajectory analysis, itself, but just the resulting graph.  Phylogenetic transformations were used to obtain random pseudo-data via RRPP and the model matrix for LS means was constructed properly, but not having the phylogenetic transformation in the last step meant the LS means were shifted away from the origin in the PC plot.  This would be a consistent (affine) shift in each RRPP permutation.

Please re-install RRPP from my Gtihub (mlcollyer/RRPP) and see if your results make sense.  Let me know if issues persist.  I will soon send an update to CRAN, but wish to test the function more first.

Sorry for the bug!

Mike

Dear geomorph community,

I am working on a phylogenetic control requested by reviewers, and I would like to know whether extended.pgls() can be combined with trajectory.analysis().

My data and design
- Multivariate shape data (48 variables) for 195 individuals of 6 species, with many individuals per species.
- Species = species (factor); Stage = an ordered three-level factor (e.g., low, medium and high wear: S1, S2, S3). The goal is to build one trajectory per species, with the three stages as trajectory points, and to compare trajectories among species (length, direction, shape).
- Phylogeny: a pruned cladogram with branch lengths assigned (Grafen), with tips matching the levels of Species.

What I did

Ordinary model (works as expected):

fit_ordinary <- procD.lm(Y ~ Species * Stage, data = my_data, iter = 999)
TA_ordinary <- trajectory.analysis(fit_ordinary, groups = my_data$Species,
                                   traj.pts = my_data$Stage, pca = TRUE)

Here the trajectory points are exactly equal to the species-by-stage means of the individual scores in the PC space returned by plot(TA_ordinary).

Phylogenetic model:

fit_phylo <- extended.pgls(Y ~ Species * Stage, data = my_data,
                           species = "Species", phy = my_tree, iter = 999)
TA_phylo <- trajectory.analysis(fit_phylo, groups = my_data$Species,
                                traj.pts = my_data$Stage, pca = TRUE)

trajectory.analysis() runs without errors, but the trajectory points do not match the data. For example, for one species (Species_A), comparing the mean of the individual scores in each stage with the trajectory point, both in the PC space of TA_phylo:

          mean of individuals       trajectory point
          PC1       PC2             PC1       PC2
S1       -0.257     0.060          -2.609     0.061
S2       -0.141     0.030          -1.802    -0.431
S3        0.249     0.134           2.423     0.585

My questions
1. Is trajectory.analysis() intended to work with objects of class lm.rrpp.ws returned by extended.pgls()? If not, is there a recommended way to run a trajectory analysis conditioned on the phylogeny when each trajectory corresponds to a different species?
2. Is there any  limitation when the groups used for the trajectories (Species) are also the species used in the phylogenetic covariance structure?

Some cells are small (for example, n = 2 individuals in a few species-by-stage combinations), in case this is relevant.

I can provide a reproducible example or share the data  if that would help.

Thank you very much for your time.

Best regards,
Ale

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] extended.pgls and trajectory.analysis
parts:
Dear Ale,

Did you change the delta argument to delta = 0.1 in the extended.pgls analysis?  It might not be clear in table 1 of our 2024 paper that we tweaked this, because we left a lot more detail to the supporting information.  I forgot to adjust this, myself, when I followed up with you, because our example in geomorph does not adjust the value.  (Maybe we should change that but an argument against it is that we do not want to inadvertently dictate that delta = 0.1 is reasonable for most analyses.)  Because the issue you had is consistent with one that I recently fixed, resulting from a typo, I had a knee-jerk reaction to think it was still an issue, but leaving the delta default (0.001, I think) caused the P = 1 result.  I’ll try to explain why this might happen.

The extended PGLS makes an n x n covariance matrix for the n individual observations, where n > N, the number of species.  If we allow the covariances among individuals to be the same as among species, the covariance matrix is singular, and any attempt to use a generalized inverse of it will result in wonky statistics.  Basically, this is the same as trying to admit that there is no variation among individuals within species in terms of their inter-individual covariances, an illogical assumption.  Therefore, the covariances must be weighted by a level of independence.  What we use as weights is exp(-delta * gamma).  If delta is 0, the weight is 1, meaning no change.  If delta tends toward 1, the weight tends toward 0, meaning independence (phylogeny does not constrain covariances).  Note that delta cannot be exactly 0 because of the aforementioned issue, so a number close to 0, like 0.001, is used as a lower limit.

The gamma parameter is for sample-size consideration.  If 1, sample size does not matter.  Otherwise it can be a ratio between 0-1 to account for sample size imbalance, as a more heavily sampled species might be expected to have more independent observations than one with poor sampling.

We used delta = 0.1 because otherwise, the covariance matrix was ill-conditioned.  What I recommend with your data is to do the following:

1. Start with the default delta.  If you get a P = 1 situation, then a BM model of evolutionary divergence completely accounts for the Species effect.
2. Creep up the delta value until you start to see a change.  This will inform you how independent your observations must be considered to detect a species effect.
3. Remember the purpose is to analyze species x “something" trends, so the species effect is not really consequential.  You would not, for example, use procD.pgls to test for a species effect for species means.  This does not make much sense.  So maybe do not worry much about the species effect.

Finally, if you change delta to 0.1, the results won’t match our 2024 paper, either. We did catch a coding issue, post-production.  This erratum though only changes the stats, not the conclusions from the test.

I might revisit this topic as a blog post later.  To be honest, this is a new frontier, so a system of best practices is still developing.  I think in a results section, one should explain what the weighting parameters were rather than assume function defaults are appropriate.

Best,
Mike

parts:
Dear Ale, and anyone else paying attention to this thread,

You asked a couple of questions earlier about trajectory analysis and limitations with using Species as a term in a model for extended PGLS.  Regarding the latter question, I felt provoked to follow-up on what I mentioned yesterday, that the results were different using different values of delta, the weight-scaling parameter for the covariance matrix.  I can confirm that this is really only an issue for the Species effect, which is a weird term to be testing when accounting for species relatedness.  Nevertheless, one might want to test for an adaptive radiation, for example, so it is not too weird to consider.  Regardless, I had not done something like create a gradient of delta to see how effects change.  (I had tuned the parameter before to rid myself of the weird Species effect, but I had not considered what might happen as a pattern to all effects.)  Now I have done that and I think it might be helpful.  Rather than just email the result, I decided to record it for posterity in blog form.  Hopefully this helps offer some guidance.  The short version is that only the species effect is volatile and only when delta is near 0.  Increasing delta causes the species effect to stabilize.  All other effects remain consistent.

Regarding the first question, I glossed over the note you made that some species are poorly sampled.  This could have some effect for trajectory analysis, if the RRPP is restricted to species blocks.  The good news is you can compare trajectories among well-sampled species without the poorly sampled species negatively impacting your inferences.  The within-species RRPP strategy makes the test robust for groups with ample replication.

Speaking of blogs, I decided to make them cool again by dedicating some space for one on my website.  There are a few other posts about things like whether to adjust P-values for posthoc tests, how awesome gpagen is, and how not all distance-based ANOVAs for multivariate data are equal (spoiler alert, our functions are pretty fast).  I am just getting started but my hope is to have a more helpful reference bank than just the google group archives.

All the best,
Mike

parts:
Dear Mike,

Thank you very much for the detailed explanation, for fixing the pairwise issue so quickly, and for taking the time to write the blog post.

I repeated your delta gradient with my own data (Species, a three-level Stage factor and their interaction, using lr_test), and the pattern is the same as in your pupfish example. The Species:Stage effect is essentially flat (Z around 9.2 to 9.4 between delta = 0.05 and 0.5), and so is the Stage effect (Z around 16). Only the Species effect is volatile: it rises from Z of about 1.3 at delta = 0.05 to about 9.9 at delta = 0.5, and at the smallest values (0.001 and 0.01) it gave P = 1 in my data as well. I plan to report the delta and gamma values I use, show the sensitivity of the Species effect in a supplementary figure, and focus the interpretation on the interaction, as you suggest.

Thanks also for clarifying the point about poorly sampled species. A few follow-up questions, if you have time:

1. In my data, a few species-by-stage cells have only 2 to 4 individuals, while other species have between 17 and 71 individuals in total. Is there a minimum number of individuals per cell that you would recommend for the trajectory points and for the pairwise comparisons of trajectories? Or would you rather flag (or exclude) the trajectories that rest on very few individuals?

2. With such unbalanced sampling, is the default gamma (weights based on sample size) a reasonable choice, or would you also check the equal-weights option as a sensitivity analysis? And would you expect the pairwise trajectory statistics (path distances, directions and shape differences) to be as stable across delta as the interaction term appears to be?

3. In my model, where the species term is in the model together with the interaction, the least-squares means that define the trajectories from extended PGLS match the ones from the ordinary least-squares model, for every delta I tried. I assume this means the phylogeny affects the inference (through the covariance used for the test statistics and the permutations) but not the trajectory points themselves. Is that the correct way to think about it?

Thank you again for all the help, and I look forward to reading more posts on your blog.

Best regards,
Ale

El viernes, 6 de noviembre de 2026 a las 19:46:00 UTC-3, mlco...@gmail.com escribió:
Dear Ale, and anyone else paying attention to this thread,

You asked a couple of questions earlier about trajectory analysis and limitations with using Species as a term in a model for extended PGLS.  Regarding the latter question, I felt provoked to follow-up on what I mentioned yesterday, that the results were different using different values of delta, the weight-scaling parameter for the covariance matrix.  I can confirm that this is really only an issue for the Species effect, which is a weird term to be testing when accounting for species relatedness.  Nevertheless, one might want to test for an adaptive radiation, for example, so it is not too weird to consider.  Regardless, I had not done something like create a gradient of delta to see how effects change.  (I had tuned the parameter before to rid myself of the weird Species effect, but I had not considered what might happen as a pattern to all effects.)  Now I have done that and I think it might be helpful.  Rather than just email the result, I decided to record it for posterity in blog form.  Hopefully this helps offer some guidance.  The short version is that only the species effect is volatile and only when delta is near 0.  Increasing delta causes the species effect to stabilize.  All other effects remain consistent.

Regarding the first question, I glossed over the note you made that some species are poorly sampled.  This could have some effect for trajectory analysis, if the RRPP is restricted to species blocks.  The good news is you can compare trajectories among well-sampled species without the poorly sampled species negatively impacting your inferences.  The within-species RRPP strategy makes the test robust for groups with ample replication.

Speaking of blogs, I decided to make them cool again by dedicating some space for one on my website.  There are a few other posts about things like whether to adjust P-values for posthoc tests, how awesome gpagen is, and how not all distance-based ANOVAs for multivariate data are equal (spoiler alert, our functions are pretty fast).  I am just getting started but my hope is to have a more helpful reference bank than just the google group archives.

All the best,
Mike

On Nov 5, 2026, at 1:43 PM, alej...@gmail.com <alej...@gmail.com> wrote:

Dear Dean and Mike,
First of all, thank you very much for your previous feedback and assistance. While the RRPP update resolved the previous issue, I have now encountered another query regarding the Species main effect in E-PGLS.
While analyzing my data, I noticed that the main effect for Species returns a p-value of 1, a very low Z-score (strongly negative), and an R2 approx 0.
To verify whether this was related to my dataset, I ran the PupFishExample-DRYAD.R script provided in the Dryad repository using the current version of RRPP/geomorph. Interestingly, running manova.update(fit) on the pupfish dataset also yields a p-value of 1.000 and Z = -31.60 for Species, whereas Table 1 in the paper reports p = 0.020 and Z = 2.221 (while the remaining terms like Sex, Population, and Species:Sex are very similar to the published table).
Could you provide some guidance on:
    1. Whether this p = 1 result for Species in the latest package version is the expected mathematical outcome?
    2. How we should properly interpret and report a p = 1 for the Species main effect in E-PGLS comparative studies when cross-species interaction terms (Species:Factor) are the main focus of interest?
Thank you again for your time, support
Best regards,
Ale


El miércoles, 4 de noviembre de 2026 a las 20:06:18 UTC-3, mlco...@gmail.com escribió:
Dear Ale, and everyone,

The issue was caused by a missing phylogenetic transformation of the model matrix used to obtain least-squares means in the RRPP::pairwise function, used within trajectory.analysis (not extended.pgls).  I am hopeful this would cause no major issues with the trajectory analysis, itself, but just the resulting graph.  Phylogenetic transformations were used to obtain random pseudo-data via RRPP and the model matrix for LS means was constructed properly, but not having the phylogenetic transformation in the last step meant the LS means were shifted away from the origin in the PC plot.  This would be a consistent (affine) shift in each RRPP permutation.

Please re-install RRPP from my Gtihub (mlcollyer/RRPP) and see if your results make sense.  Let me know if issues persist.  I will soon send an update to CRAN, but wish to test the function more first.

Sorry for the bug!

Mike

Dear geomorph community,

I am working on a phylogenetic control requested by reviewers, and I would like to know whether extended.pgls() can be combined with trajectory.analysis().

My data and design
- Multivariate shape data (48 variables) for 195 individuals of 6 species, with many individuals per species.
- Species = species (factor); Stage = an ordered three-level factor (e.g., low, medium and high wear: S1, S2, S3). The goal is to build one trajectory per species, with the three stages as trajectory points, and to compare trajectories among species (length, direction, shape).
- Phylogeny: a pruned cladogram with branch lengths assigned (Grafen), with tips matching the levels of Species.

What I did

Ordinary model (works as expected):

fit_ordinary <- procD.lm(Y ~ Species * Stage, data = my_data, iter = 999)
TA_ordinary <- trajectory.analysis(fit_ordinary, groups = my_data$Species,
                                   traj.pts = my_data$Stage, pca = TRUE)

Here the trajectory points are exactly equal to the species-by-stage means of the individual scores in the PC space returned by plot(TA_ordinary).

Phylogenetic model:

fit_phylo <- extended.pgls(Y ~ Species * Stage, data = my_data,
                           species = "Species", phy = my_tree, iter = 999)
TA_phylo <- trajectory.analysis(fit_phylo, groups = my_data$Species,
                                traj.pts = my_data$Stage, pca = TRUE)

trajectory.analysis() runs without errors, but the trajectory points do not match the data. For example, for one species (Species_A), comparing the mean of the individual scores in each stage with the trajectory point, both in the PC space of TA_phylo:

          mean of individuals       trajectory point
          PC1       PC2             PC1       PC2
S1       -0.257     0.060          -2.609     0.061
S2       -0.141     0.030          -1.802    -0.431
S3        0.249     0.134           2.423     0.585

My questions
1. Is trajectory.analysis() intended to work with objects of class lm.rrpp.ws returned by extended.pgls()? If not, is there a recommended way to run a trajectory analysis conditioned on the phylogeny when each trajectory corresponds to a different species?
2. Is there any  limitation when the groups used for the trajectories (Species) are also the species used in the phylogenetic covariance structure?

Some cells are small (for example, n = 2 individuals in a few species-by-stage combinations), in case this is relevant.

I can provide a reproducible example or share the data  if that would help.

Thank you very much for your time.

Best regards,
Ale
